articles.title: Next.js 16 updateTag vs revalidateTag: What Changed
articles.description: Next.js 16 deprecated revalidateTag's single-argument call and added updateTag. What the new profile argument changes, plus a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
Your team upgrades to Next.js 16, the build passes, and nothing in the diff touches caching. A week later, publishing a blog post starts taking noticeably longer — not to save, but for the next reader to see it. Somewhere in a Server Action sits a line nobody touched: revalidateTag('posts'). It still runs. It just does something different now.

That line used to mark the posts tag stale and move on — the next visitor got the old page instantly while Next.js refreshed it in the background. In Next.js 16, the same one-argument call is deprecated, and its behavior changed to match an immediate, blocking cache miss: the next request to anything tagged posts now waits for fresh data before it renders. No error, no red build — just a slower app and a cache-invalidation story that quietly inverted.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain exactly what changed in revalidateTag's signature in Next.js 16, and why old, un-migrated calls now behave differently than they did in 15
  • Use the new profile argument ("max", a custom cacheLife name, or { expire }) to choose stale-while-revalidate on purpose instead of by accident
  • Reach for updateTag correctly — and know the one restriction that makes it unusable outside a Server Action
  • Pick the right tool for three real situations: a Server Action after a write, a webhook Route Handler, and "the reader must see their own change immediately"
  • Read the TypeScript error a bare revalidateTag(tag) now produces, and migrate it correctly

Who this is for

You've used revalidateTag or cacheTag in an App Router project before — maybe to invalidate a list page after a mutation. You don't need to have used Cache Components; this article explains the pieces it touches as it goes.

This article is written against Next.js 16.4 (verified against the framework's own next/cache API documentation and the v16.0.0 release notes from October 2025, where both the new updateTag function and revalidateTag's new signature shipped). Where the pre-16 behavior differs, it's stated explicitly rather than assumed.

Table of contents

  • The problem: a call that still compiles, now does less for free
  • The mental model: two knobs, not one
  • Stage 1: what the deprecated call actually does now
  • Stage 2: revalidateTag(tag, "max") — keeping the old UX, on purpose
  • Stage 3: updateTag — read-your-own-write, from a Server Action only
  • Stage 4: the webhook case, where updateTag isn't an option
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet

The problem: a call that still compiles, now does less for free

Here's a Server Action that was correct in Next.js 15 and is still, technically, legal code in 16:

// app/actions.ts — written for Next.js 15
'use server';

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function publishPost(formData: FormData) {
  await db.posts.create({ title: formData.get('title') });
  revalidateTag('posts'); // one argument — this was the whole API
}

In Next.js 15, this marked every cache entry tagged posts as stale. It didn't refresh anything immediately. The next request that touched a posts-tagged entry got served the stale copy instantly, while Next.js regenerated it in the background — the standard stale-while-revalidate shape, and the reason revalidation never caused a visible slowdown.

In Next.js 16, the same call is deprecated, and its documented behavior now matches passing { expire: 0 } explicitly: the tag's cached entries lose their stale grace period entirely, so the next request becomes a blocking cache miss — it waits for the data to be refetched before it can render anything. If you're on TypeScript with the current next types, you'll actually see this before it ships: the one-argument call no longer type-checks, because revalidateTag's signature now requires a second argument. A plain JavaScript project, or one with type errors suppressed, won't see anything — just a page that got slower for no reason the diff explains.

The mental model: two knobs, not one

The mental model: before Next.js 16, "revalidate this tag" was one decision — stale now, refreshed lazily, always. Next.js 16 splits that into two independent knobs, and makes you set both:

  1. Which tag is now out of date. Unchanged — you still assign tags with cacheTag('posts') inside a 'use cache' function, or the next: { tags: [...] } option on fetch.
  2. How long is a stale copy still acceptable to serve while fresh data loads. This is the new profile argument. "max" means "basically forever" (a one-year window) — in practice, the next visitor always gets the stale copy, and it's a backstage reader who ever sees a cache miss. { expire: 0 } means "never" — the very next request must wait. Anything in between is a named cacheLife profile ("hours", "days", …) or a custom { expire: n } in seconds.

updateTag is the same second knob pinned permanently to { expire: 0 }, plus one restriction that revalidateTag doesn't have: it only runs from inside a Server Action. That restriction is the point — it exists for the one case where "the next request should see this" actually means "the request I'm about to send back to the browser that just wrote this should see this," which is a guarantee only a Server Action's own round trip can make.

Stage 1: what the deprecated call actually does now

Don't write the bare call going forward — but it's worth seeing exactly what it degrades to, since it's the code every pre-16 App Router project already has:

// Deprecated as of Next.js 16 — still "works," but not the way it used to
revalidateTag('posts');
// ...is now read as:
revalidateTag('posts', { expire: 0 });

Both forms tell Next.js: forget the stale window entirely, and make the next request pay for a fresh fetch. The difference from 15 isn't the tag, isn't the function name — it's that this was never the default behavior before, and now it quietly is.

Stage 2: revalidateTag(tag, "max") — keeping the old UX, on purpose

Most of the time, the 15-era experience — instant stale response, quiet background refresh — is still what you want. In 16 you ask for it explicitly:

// app/actions.ts
'use server';

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function publishPost(formData: FormData) {
  await db.posts.create({ title: formData.get('title') });
  revalidateTag('posts', 'max'); // stale-while-revalidate, same shape as pre-16 default
}

Key concept: "max" isn't a special case bolted onto revalidateTag — it's the same named profile cacheLife('max') uses elsewhere (a 30-day background-refresh window, one-year outer expiry). The profile argument accepts any cacheLife profile name or a { expire } object; "max" is simply the one that reproduces the old always-stale-while-revalidating default most closely.

This one-line migration is also the fix for the TypeScript error from Stage 1 — it's the smallest change that both satisfies the new signature and keeps the behavior your app already shipped with.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stage 3: updateTag — read-your-own-write, from a Server Action only

Some flows need the opposite of stale-while-revalidate: the person who just wrote the data must see it on their very next page load, not "eventually." That's what updateTag is for:

// app/actions.ts
'use server';

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function publishPost(formData: FormData) {
  const post = await db.posts.create({ title: formData.get('title') });
  updateTag('posts');          // the list page the author is about to land on
  updateTag(`post-${post.id}`); // the detail page too, if it's tagged separately
  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`);
}

updateTag(tag) takes no second argument — it's always an immediate expiry, by design, because "read your own write" has exactly one acceptable staleness window: none. Call it from anywhere else — a Route Handler, a Client Component, proxy.ts — and it throws. That's not a bug to work around; it's the signal that you're in the wrong place for a read-your-own-write guarantee and should reach for revalidateTag instead.

Key concept: updateTag and revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 0 }) end up invalidating the same cache entries the same way. The difference is entirely about where you're allowed to call them and what that implies: updateTag's restriction to Server Actions is what lets Next.js guarantee the very next render — the one already in flight back to that same browser — sees the fresh data.

Stage 4: the webhook case, where updateTag isn't an option

A CMS webhook that fires when an editor publishes from a completely separate system has no Server Action to call updateTag from — it's a Route Handler, reached by an HTTP request from somewhere else entirely:

// app/api/revalidate/route.ts
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function POST(request: NextRequest) {
  const { tag, secret } = await request.json();
  if (secret !== process.env.REVALIDATE_SECRET) {
    return Response.json({ revalidated: false }, { status: 401 });
  }
  revalidateTag(tag, 'max');
  return Response.json({ revalidated: true, now: Date.now() });
}

revalidateTag works in both Server Actions and Route Handlers; updateTag works in neither except the former. For a webhook, 'max' is almost always right — the editor's CMS doesn't need to see the update instantly, your readers do, and stale-while-revalidate means nobody's request ever blocks on it. Reach for { expire: 0 } only if the content being invalidated must never be served stale again even once — a takedown, a price correction, something wrong enough that one more stale read is a real cost.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • The deprecated one-argument call "works only if TypeScript errors are suppressed." That's the documentation's own description of its current status — the type signature now requires profile, so a strict TypeScript build already fails on it. If your build is green on a bare revalidateTag(tag) today, either you're on plain JavaScript or something in your config is swallowing the type error; either way, the runtime behavior already changed.
  • Tags are case-sensitive and capped at 256 characters. A tag longer than that is never actually attached to anything, so revalidating it does nothing — and nothing tells you it silently no-op'd.
  • A tag has to exist before you can invalidate it. cacheTag('posts') inside a 'use cache' function, or fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['posts'] } }), is what attaches the tag in the first place. Calling revalidateTag('posts') for a tag nothing ever assigned is a legal, silent no-op.
  • The revalidation runs on the next request, not on the call itself. revalidateTag/updateTag mark data stale or expired; they don't reach out and regenerate it synchronously at call time. A script that calls revalidateTag for a thousand tags in a loop doesn't do a thousand regenerations right then — it marks a thousand tags, and each one regenerates whenever its own next request arrives.
  • revalidateTag invalidates by tag across every page that uses it; revalidatePath invalidates one path. They're not competitors — a mutation that affects a shared list (tag-based) and a specific detail page (path-based) commonly needs both.
  • None of these run in proxy.ts or a Client Component. Cache invalidation is a server-side, request-scoped operation; both functions throw outside a Server Action or Route Handler.

Best practices

  • Default to revalidateTag(tag, 'max') for anything a normal visitor reads. It reproduces the stale-while-revalidate experience every pre-16 app already had, and it's almost never the wrong call for a list page, a feed, or anything else where "a few seconds old" is indistinguishable from fresh.
  • Reserve updateTag for the exact read-your-own-write moment — right after a Server Action's own mutation, on the page that same action is about to redirect to. Don't reach for it as a general-purpose "make this fresher" tool; that's what the profile argument on revalidateTag is for.
  • Migrate the bare revalidateTag(tag) calls first, deliberately, not by auto-fixing them to { expire: 0 }. The codemod or a quick find-and-replace will make the type error go away either way, but silently keeping the new blocking behavior everywhere is exactly the slowdown this article opened with. Decide 'max' vs { expire: 0 } per call site.
  • Keep webhook-triggered invalidation on revalidateTag, always. updateTag's Server-Action-only restriction isn't a gap to route around with a trick — treat it as confirmation you're using the right tool for an external trigger.
  • Pair tag-based and path-based invalidation when a mutation really touches both. A single revalidateTag call doesn't help a page that was only ever cached by path.

FAQ

Why did revalidateTag('posts') get slower after I upgraded to Next.js 16?

It didn't get slower by accident — its documented behavior changed. The one-argument form is deprecated and now matches { expire: 0 }: an immediate expiry instead of the old lazy, stale-while-revalidate refresh. Add 'max' as a second argument to restore the pre-16 behavior on purpose.

Is revalidateTag being removed?

Not entirely. The one-argument call is deprecated and documented as something that "may be removed in a future version," but revalidateTag(tag, profile) with an explicit profile is the current, supported API — it isn't going anywhere.

Can I call updateTag from a Route Handler?

No. It only runs inside a Server Action, and calling it anywhere else — a Route Handler, a Client Component, proxy.ts — throws. Use revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 0 }) there instead if you need the same immediate-expiry behavior outside a Server Action.

What profile should I pass for a webhook that revalidates on publish?

'max' almost always. The system calling the webhook (a CMS, a headless commerce backend) doesn't need the new data to appear instantly from its own point of view — your readers do, and 'max' means they always get an instant, cached response while Next.js refreshes it behind the scenes.

Does this change anything about how tags are assigned?

No. cacheTag() inside a 'use cache' function and the next: { tags: [...] } option on fetch work exactly as before. What changed is only the second half of the pair — how you tell Next.js to treat a tag's existing cached data as stale.

Cheat sheet

Situation Call Where it runs
Keep pre-16 behavior (stale-while-revalidate) revalidateTag(tag, 'max') Server Action or Route Handler
Custom staleness window revalidateTag(tag, 'hours') or revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 3600 }) Server Action or Route Handler
Reader must see their own write immediately updateTag(tag) Server Action only — throws elsewhere
Immediate expiry, outside a Server Action (e.g. a webhook) revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 0 }) Route Handler
⚠️ Old one-argument call revalidateTag(tag) Deprecated — now behaves like { expire: 0 }, and fails to type-check under current next types
Invalidate a specific route instead of a tag revalidatePath(path) Server Action or Route Handler 
// The decision, as code
'use server';
import { revalidateTag, updateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function publishPost(formData: FormData) {
  const post = await db.posts.create({ title: formData.get('title') });

  // Everyone else: stale is fine, never block a request for it.
  revalidateTag('posts', 'max');

  // The author, about to be redirected to the post they just wrote:
  // they must see it now, not the pre-write cached version.
  updateTag(`post-${post.id}`);

  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`);
}

Key takeaways

  • Next.js 16 split "revalidate this tag" into two decisions: which tag is stale, and how long a stale copy may still be served. The second one is a required argument now, not an implicit default.
  • The bare revalidateTag(tag) call is deprecated and now behaves like { expire: 0 } — an immediate, blocking cache miss — which is the opposite of the lazy stale-while-revalidate behavior it had in 15.
  • revalidateTag(tag, 'max') is the one-line migration that restores the old, reader-friendly default on purpose.
  • updateTag exists for exactly one job — the writer seeing their own change on the very next render — and that job is why it's restricted to Server Actions only.
  • Webhooks and anything outside a Server Action stay on revalidateTag; there's no version of updateTag for that context, by design.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Back to that slow publish button

The team in the opening didn't ship a bug — they shipped code that was correct for the Next.js version it was written against, and the ground moved under one function call during an upgrade that otherwise looked clean. The fix was one argument: revalidateTag('posts', 'max') to get the old behavior back, and updateTag reserved for the one page where "eventually" was never good enough.

If cacheTag, cacheLife, and the static-shell-vs-streaming split underneath all of this are new to you, Next.js Cache Components Explained builds that model from the ground up. For the mutation side of this same flow — validating the FormData, the CSRF guarantees a Server Action gives you for free, and the redirect() gotcha — see Next.js Server Actions: Mutations & Security. And if your cache entries are built from a Route Handler's own GET rather than a Server Component, Next.js Route Handlers: GET Stopped Caching in 15 covers the other half of the 15-to-16 caching story.

articles.description: I've used breakpoints, profilers, and all the fancy devtools. But when something breaks at 1 AM, my...
articles.body_html:
I've used breakpoints, profilers, and all the fancy devtools. But when something breaks at 1 AM, my first move is still:

console.log("here");
console.log("here 2");
console.log("WHY IS THIS UNDEFINED");

It's not pretty, but it works. Here's what I've noticed over time:

  • Writing a log forces me to state what I expect. To log a value, I first have to decide what it should be at that line.
  • It works everywhere. Every language, every stack, zero setup.
  • The bug often shows up while I'm typing the log. Half the time I find it before running anything.

Where it stops working

The rule I follow now: if I've added more than 5 logs, I'm guessing, not debugging.

At that point the logs have stopped answering questions and started adding noise. That's the moment to stop and step through the code with a real debugger, where I can inspect state, watch the call stack, and see exactly where the value changes.

Print debugging isn't the problem

Used on purpose, console.log is a fast way to test a hypothesis. The trouble starts when it replaces thinking.

Print debugging isn't the problem. Not knowing when to stop is.

Make empty what is already empty. Let doubt breed inside doubt.
— The 36 Stratagems, The Empty Fort Strategy

Previously on this series:

#19: Mark Found His AI Audit Method in a Training Manual. He Left a Trap in His Report. "Entry's gone. Two weeks. Don't reach out. I'll find you."

#21: The AI Thought P Was Still Alive. P Was Already Gone. The entry became a shell. P fed it data, moved the real thing to another segment.

#29: Leo Counted 164 Nodes. That night, one more row belonged to no batch. It came, looked, and left.

#31: Lena Took the Seat. Five conditions. Forty minutes. Zero friction.

Empty

The two weeks specified in the note had long since passed.

P went out rarely. Most days it was the shop on the corner: water, two boxes of frozen food. Twelve minutes each way, same route, never looking up. Then the door locked, the curtains drawn, the screen on.

On the ninth day, P opened the send window once.

The draft was still there. The pointer hovered over Send. It stayed there a while. Then the window closed.

On the other side, the field still read reclaim_state = UNKNOWN.

Day ten. Day eleven. The window didn't open again.

A few days later it started raining in the morning. Not hard. Water gathered on the glass, the buildings behind it went grey, only the row of lights along the top still visible.

An offline snapshot sat in the middle of the screen, written before the observation port shut down. Nothing after that. By then the entry had already been swapped for a shell. The shell held nothing of P's. It was still answering health checks from outside.

# offline snapshot — captured before observation-port shutdown
healthcheck        = 200
probe_interval     = 900s
probe_source       = 10.44.8.6   not self
control_plane      = detached
data_request       = timeout
reclaim_state      = UNKNOWN

P put the cursor on the probe_source line.

probe_source = not self. Someone asked about this shell every fifteen minutes. Not P.

P stayed on that line a while. Nothing else on screen moved. The clock in the corner ticked. Downstairs a shopping cart went past, a wheel caught in a seam and bumped twice, the sound squeezing through the gap in the frame, then fading.

P opened the connection settings. The address was still there. The credentials were still there. Neither had been touched.

The cursor moved to the confirmation button and stopped. The green of the screen came up off the glass and landed on the back of a hand.

A few seconds later, P closed the window.

The old entry's observation port was already shut. The backup had been checked once at the start, then shut too.

Since then, P had sent nothing to that address.

A temporary file, four lines.

reconnect:
  state information    potentially available
  new activity record  unavoidable
  decision             no

Saved. The old settings moved out of the working directory, into the offline archive. P glanced at the filename on the way and left it untouched.

The phone lay face down to the right of the keyboard. P opened the thread with Mark. The last exchange ended before the note. Nothing after it.

P typed nothing.

Outside a car went through standing water, the sound dragging. P turned the phone over, set it down. Then opened the file that had stayed open for weeks and entered one line from the snapshot: probe_interval = 900s.

Surfacing

Week three. P set up a read-only subscription on the outbound side. Receive. No transmission.

The table started at a dozen entries, several dozen more the next day, and by the third night it was full. Every entry came with its own certificate.

Those addresses were not in P's archive.

The subscription only read. To look at one, P needed another path.

Out of the drawer, a cellular router, rented by the day, SIM included. Plugged in, configured as the sole egress path.

P chose one address and initiated a single handshake.

The certificate was self-signed. Its CN contained a domain name.

P looked up the domain's registration. The registrant was a medical device company.

Disconnected. Packed away.

The list of addresses kept growing. P wrote them down and left them there.

The Handover

10.44.8.6 had been in front of P many times. Always on the probe_source line. Never changed. Over the next few days, P looked into it. First the route.

$ ip route get 10.44.8.6
10.44.8.6 via 10.44.8.1 dev tun2 src 10.44.8.2

P switched windows and opened the local subnet-label cache.

# local subnet-label cache
10.44.8.0/29 -> BLOOM-GW   tagged day-762

BLOOM-GW.

P had typed that label years earlier, when the line was built. The private block was P's numbering. The rack IDs were the provider's. This table was where the two met.

In the provider's public sublease filings, seven racks changed tenants in the same quarter. The provider had also published an annual customer-change notice on its site. Twelve pages of PDF. The first eleven pages were image scans; the last was a single table.

Seven rows. A rack ID, a previous tenant, a new tenant. Seven rows, not one out of place. Seven new tenants, checked one by one.

On the seventh, P found that rack ID in another public record. Vacant.

Four were established. Three were shells. All three registered less than a year earlier, one name on the shareholder list, addresses overlapping with the others'.

One of the three took longer to trace. Registered six months earlier, little capital, a single office address in the public file. P put the address into a map.

Singapore. The last time P had seen that name, it was in a message to Mark: "Your report was read. From a Singapore IP."

A building on the map, sharing a ground-level parking lot with the one next door.

On the seventh floor of the neighboring building, one company was on ACL's public certification list.

P added that too, at the bottom of the same file.

Seven racks. Seven contracts. Three markets.

Handed over in order. The legal filings in the public archive were standard, spelling out the limits of each party's obligations. No accusations. No threats. The seven contracts were signed over thirty-one days, first to last, no gap in the middle. The last one was signed last week.

The address allocation table was updated too. Both records less than a week apart.

P read all of it for a long time.

The withdrawal was real.

Seven contracts, seven racks, the notices, the update records, the timestamps. All of it outside, where anyone could look.

P added a line to the file. The date, seven contracts, seven companies, the address with the shared parking lot, in one line. Below it, in plain words: a possible connection.

The cursor blinked after the period. P went back to page one. The 900 seconds were still there.

One Look

Week five. The source of the 900 seconds still had no answer.

P went back over the two relabeled rack IDs in the allocation table. One endpoint had 443 open. A separate public service directory listed the endpoint as HTTPS.

P didn't connect from this machine. Out of the drawer, the router.

Plugged in, left to come up, configured as the sole egress path.

Then the policy, one line at a time. Halfway through, P stopped and deleted two lines.

The probe. The retry.

What was left was one action. One handshake. Touch nothing.

# one-shot observation — policy
target            = <reassigned range endpoint>
retry             = off
application_data  = off
tls_session_resumption = off
egress            = leased isolated uplink (one day)

Connected.

P still had the shell certificate's serial number and issue date. If the device at this address came from the same batch, the certificates should have been issued around the same time.

subject      = CN=bloom-gw-07
issuer       = CN=bloom-gw-07
serial       = 4C:71:9A:…:0E
not_before   = (eleven days later than the shell's)
not_after    = (not yet expired)
san          = none

Self-signed. No SAN.

Eleven days.

P wrote the serial down and disconnected.

19:41:07.

That didn't fall on any of the twenty-one intervals.

# result
tls_session      = complete
client_cert      = none
application_data = none
repeat_attempts  = 0

No second attempt.

P disconnected the router and pulled the plug. The lights went out together.

The device ran a few seconds, then went quiet. Then it went into the bag, and the bag zipped. A spare patch cable and two adapters in there too, both old, the corners worn white.

After pulling it, P didn't move right away. Checked the connection list first, made sure the session was down with nothing half-open left. Then the routing table, the default route back where it belonged. Then the temp capture directory. One file in it.

Deleted.

P wrote the serial down again. That same day, P opened a page saved a few days earlier, the Zurich AI Policy Center site. ACL's public assessment material mentioned it. The council operated under it.

The membership page listed the founding industry seats. Twelve. The twelfth was marked to be filled.

P looked once, and closed it.

Nine Hundred Seconds

A few days later, P went back to page one. The 900 seconds were still there.

P pulled up the local copy saved before the port shut. Twenty-two checks, timestamps in a line, all of them before the shutdown. Arrival times, not scheduled times, carried out to three decimals. Twenty-one intervals.

P ran it through a tool.

900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / …

Twenty-one values. All the same.

P went through all twenty-two again. Same. Again. Same. The numbers formed a straight line down the page.

Routine monitoring records usually have some jitter. Network latency, machine load, clock drift.

This had none.

Not a millisecond off.

P looked up the provider's operations doc. On the public page: health checks run every fifteen minutes. Standard cadence.

900 seconds.

It matched.

The doc was about racks. Temperature, power, fans, port state.

P stared at the numbers a while, then added a line at the top of the file: routine data-center inspection, BLOOM-GW reassigned block.

After writing it, P added one more underneath. The interval has no jitter.

The desk lamp went off. Only the screen was left, its light across the desk, a white line along the edge of the keyboard.

The twenty-two timestamps sat in neat rows. P ran a finger down the trackpad from top to bottom, then back.

Outside, not yet dawn. A garbage truck stopped at the corner, the arm came up, emptied a bin, put it back. Under ten seconds.

Two-story wooden buildings on both sides, painted over more than once, one colour under another. Behind them the glass towers stepped back floor by floor, the top few in fog.

P saved the file and closed the window.

The Third Cup

The rain started again that day. Not hard. A thin sound on the umbrella.

P got off at an intersection and walked. A little over two kilometers, twenty minutes. Around a corner, a stop outside a shop still open, no going in, just standing under the awning watching traffic. At the light, P stood behind the crowd. Took two seconds after green to move.

Before going in, P looked at the back table.

Empty.

P pushed the door. The bell went, the damp cold came in with it, stopped at the threshold, and the heat pushed it back.

The counter was wood, old. A grinder, a machine, a dish for change.

Behind it, someone was wiping a cup. Slow. The cloth around the rim, down the side, back to the rim, onto the shelf.

A glance up. No question asked. Then turned, took a cup, ground, tamped.

The grinder ran two seconds. A faint smell of coffee, gone fast.

The back table was empty.

P sat. Coat over the chair back, phone on the right, face down.

Old chair. It creaked going down and coming up. P pulled it in a little, lifting it so it wouldn't drag.

The espresso came, hot. A thin mist on the cup, gone quickly. Paper coaster, an old ring on it.

P took one sip and put it down.

A bus went past the window, the cabin lights sliding across the glass, lighting the empty seat opposite for a moment, then gone.

At the far end of the counter, someone sat with an Americano, down to the bottom, the cup not pushed back.

The window seat was empty. No cup on that table.

Two people came in and sat near the door, voices low, a laugh now and then. Behind the counter, the cups went back one at a time, starting from the outside and working in.

The speaker in the corner was on, low, a woman singing, the words not clear. Someone shook out an umbrella at the door. Three drops on the mat.

P's phone stayed dark.

Half an hour.

More than half the cup left. The coffee had gone from hot to warm. The mist on the rim was gone.

P's finger stopped on the rim, then came back.

The two near the door left first. Stood, pushed the chairs in, carried their cups up, gone.

The one at the counter moved after. Phone face down, stood, money under the cup, walked to the door. As the customer passed P's table, neither looked at the other.

The shop had the window lights and one person behind the counter, drying a cup.

P put the coat on and stood. The chair leg scraped once. Phone into the inner pocket.

The napkin stayed under the cup. The money lay beside it, pinning one corner, exact, one cup, no tip.

The person behind the counter came for the money. Looked at the cup. Looked under the napkin. Said nothing, took the money to the dish, stepped away.

The cup stayed on the table.

The door opened, some of the heat went out with it, the cold filled the gap. The bell again.

The rain had stopped before P went out. P walked to the corner, stopped, looked back.

A street and a pane of glass between. Not clear from there. A figure was going in, walked to the far end of the counter, sat, back to the door.

Before sitting down, the figure turned slightly to one side.

P stopped.

She took a laptop from her bag. The screen lit and put a small white patch on her profile.

The road was black with rain, holding the streetlights and the light from inside. Water still on the glass, pulling the figure into a blurred double.

Behind the counter, the half-wiped cup went down. One came from the innermost part of the shelf. Ground, tamped.

By the time the cup went in front of her, she was facing the back table.

On that table sat a cup of unfinished espresso.

P put both hands in the coat pockets, turned, walked toward the intersection. Didn't look again.

At the corner. Red.

P took the phone out and opened the blank note on top.

Typed:

The withdrawal was real.

Before locking it, the line above, written days earlier:

The interval has no jitter.

Still there. P didn't delete it.

Locked it, put it away.

The light changed, people started moving. P didn't.

Red. Green. Red.

The next night. The same corner.

P took the phone out.

The screen was on. The saved route was still there. The recipient had not changed. P went through it once, and the encryption check came back clean.

There was an old draft in the field. P deleted it.

Typed again.

Two words.

"I'm back."

Checked the receiver. Sent.

The status went to SENT.

The sender field held a single letter.

P put the phone away. Across the street the red light lay in the standing water, went green a few seconds later, and a passing car cut the red on the road in half.

P walked into the intersection. The phone didn't light again.

That's The Empty Fort Strategy. The fort is empty. Whoever looks will stand guard for it.

articles.title: How I finally understood the Interface Segregation Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Letter four of five. Last post we broke a fat PaymentMethod into PaymentMethod +...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Letter four of five. Last post we broke a fat PaymentMethod into PaymentMethod + Refundable and the compiler started catching our bugs. Today we take that idea and make it the whole show.

The I: Interface Segregation Principle. The one with the longest name and the shortest explanation.

The What

Official words:

No code should be forced to depend on methods it does not use.

That's... actually pretty readable for once. Let me still make it concrete.

An interface is a menu. ISP says: don't hand someone a 40-item menu when they came in for coffee. Give them the coffee menu.

Let's build a smart home to see what happens when the menu gets too big.

The How

We start with a lamp and a speaker. The team decides every device should implement one common interface so the app can treat them all the same. Reasonable!

// src/smart-device.ts
export interface SmartDevice {
  turnOn(): void
  turnOff(): void
  setTemperature(celsius: number): void
  play(track: string): void
  pause(): void
  setBrightness(percent: number): void
}

Now let's implement the lamp:

// src/lamp.ts
import type { SmartDevice } from './smart-device.js'

export class Lamp implements SmartDevice {
  private on = false

  turnOn() {
    this.on = true
    console.log('💡 lamp on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    this.on = false
    console.log('💡 lamp off')
  }

  setBrightness(percent: number) {
    console.log(`💡 brightness ${percent}%`)
  }

  setTemperature() {
    throw new Error('A lamp has no thermostat')
  }

  play() {
    throw new Error('A lamp cannot play music')
  }

  pause() {
    throw new Error('A lamp cannot pause music')
  }
}

Three real methods. Three methods that exist only to throw. The lamp is 50% apology.

The speaker is the same story in reverse: play() and pause() are real, setBrightness() and setTemperature() are throws. And the thermostat implements six methods to use one.

Now the app layer. We want a "good night" routine that turns everything off:

// src/routines.ts
import type { SmartDevice } from './smart-device.js'

export function goodNight(devices: SmartDevice[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.turnOff()
  }
}

Works. But then someone writes "movie mode":

export function movieMode(devices: SmartDevice[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.setBrightness(20)
    device.play('intro.mp3')
  }
}

Run it with a lamp in the list and play() throws. Run it with a speaker and setBrightness() throws. The function signature says "give me any SmartDevice" and that's a lie. If you read the last post, you just spotted a Liskov violation. ISP is how we stop creating them.

And one more pain you don't see until month three: add lockDoor() to SmartDevice for the new smart lock and every existing device, including the lamp, has to grow another throwing method. One interface change, twelve files touched. Ouch.

Step 1: split the menu by capability

What can devices actually do? Let's list the verbs and group them:

// src/capabilities.ts
export interface Switchable {
  turnOn(): void
  turnOff(): void
}

export interface Dimmable {
  setBrightness(percent: number): void
}

export interface Thermostat {
  setTemperature(celsius: number): void
}

export interface MediaPlayer {
  play(track: string): void
  pause(): void
}

Four tiny interfaces. Each one is a single idea.

Step 2: devices pick what they can honestly do 

// src/lamp.ts
import type { Switchable, Dimmable } from './capabilities.js'

export class Lamp implements Switchable, Dimmable {
  turnOn() {
    console.log('💡 lamp on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    console.log('💡 lamp off')
  }

  setBrightness(percent: number) {
    console.log(`💡 brightness ${percent}%`)
  }
}

// src/speaker.ts
import type { Switchable, MediaPlayer } from './capabilities.js'

export class Speaker implements Switchable, MediaPlayer {
  turnOn() {
    console.log('🔊 speaker on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    console.log('🔊 speaker off')
  }

  play(track: string) {
    console.log(`🔊 playing ${track}`)
  }

  pause() {
    console.log('🔊 paused')
  }
}

Zero throws. The lamp is 100% lamp.

Step 3: routines ask for the capability they use 

// src/routines.ts
import type { Switchable, Dimmable, MediaPlayer } from './capabilities.js'

export function goodNight(devices: Switchable[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.turnOff()
  }
}

export function movieMode(lights: Dimmable[], players: MediaPlayer[]) {
  for (const light of lights) {
    light.setBrightness(20)
  }
  for (const player of players) {
    player.play('intro.mp3')
  }
}

// src/main.ts
import { Lamp } from './lamp.js'
import { Speaker } from './speaker.js'
import { goodNight, movieMode } from './routines.js'

const lamp = new Lamp()
const speaker = new Speaker()

movieMode([lamp], [speaker])
goodNight([lamp, speaker])

Output:

💡 brightness 20%
🔊 playing intro.mp3
💡 lamp off
🔊 speaker off

Try to sneak the speaker into the lights array and TypeScript stops you before you even hit save. 🛑

Step 4: the smart lock test

New device, new capability:

// src/capabilities.ts
export interface Lockable {
  lock(): void
  unlock(): void
}

// src/door-lock.ts
import type { Lockable } from './capabilities.js'

export class DoorLock implements Lockable {
  lock() {
    console.log('🔒 locked')
  }

  unlock() {
    console.log('🔓 unlocked')
  }
}

Files touched besides the new ones: zero. The lamp didn't even blink.

The Why

  • No more apology methods. If a class throws "not supported", the interface was too fat. Split it until every implementation is honest.
  • Functions say exactly what they need. goodNight(devices: Switchable[]) tells you in the signature that it only flips switches. Documentation for free.
  • Adding a capability doesn't ripple. New interface, new class, done. Existing devices are untouched.
  • Tests get tiny. Want to test goodNight()? Pass an object with turnOn and turnOff. You don't need to fake six methods to test two.
  • It is cheap in TypeScript. Interfaces compile to nothing. Four small ones cost exactly as much as one big one: zero bytes.

Rule of thumb: if you can't describe an interface in one short sentence ("something you can switch on and off"), it's probably two interfaces.

The Goodbye

Four down. The final letter is the D, Dependency Inversion, and it's the one that ties the whole series together. If you've read my post about loosely coupled modules you already have a head start.

Until then: find an interface with more than five methods and ask it, politely, what it really wants to be. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: The CRDT That Throws Itself Away: Inside Eg-walker
articles.description: Here's a number from a recent systems paper that stopped me cold.  Take the real editing history of...
articles.body_html:
Here's a number from a recent systems paper that stopped me cold.

Take the real editing history of Git's own Makefile, reconstructed from the Git repository, with its many authors and branches. Merge it with a classic Operational Transformation algorithm, and it takes one hour. Merge it with an algorithm called Eg-walker, and it takes 24 milliseconds.

Eg-walker comes from Joseph Gentle and Martin Kleppmann, in the paper Collaborative Text Editing with Eg-walker: Better, Faster, Smaller, presented at EuroSys 2025. What makes it interesting isn't just the speed. It's the trick behind it: a CRDT that only exists for the duration of a merge and is then thrown away.

If you've worked with collaborative editing, you know the trade-off this breaks. Let's look at how.

The trade-off everyone has lived with

There are two families of algorithms for collaborative text.

Operational Transformation (OT) stores the document as plain text and transforms concurrent operations against each other. It's memory-light and loads instantly, which is why Google Docs, Microsoft Office, and Overleaf use it. The problem is merging. If two users each made n edits while apart, every edit from one side has to be transformed against every edit from the other. That's at least O(n²), and some OT algorithms are cubic or worse. Fine for real-time typing with small n. Painful for offline work or long-running branches.

CRDTs give every character a unique ID and store positions relative to other IDs. Merging long branches is fine, and they work peer-to-peer. But that metadata has to be loaded from disk and held in memory the entire time a document is open, even when nobody else is editing. The paper measured that even the best CRDTs today use more than ten times the memory of OT just to view and edit a document.

So you pick: slow merges, or heavy documents.

Insight 1: store the history, not the state

Eg-walker starts by changing what gets stored and replicated.

Instead of CRDT metadata, every replica keeps an event graph: a DAG of every edit, where each event holds three things. An ID, the IDs of its parent events, and the operation exactly as the user performed it. That means plain index-based operations like Insert(3, "l") or Delete(1), never transformed, never rewritten.

If that sounds like Git, it should. The parents of an event record what its author had seen when they made it. Two events are concurrent if neither is an ancestor of the other, just like two commits on different branches.

This gives a clean definition of the problem. The document is simply:

document = replay(eventGraph)

where replay is a deterministic function. Any two replicas with the same set of events must produce the same document. Everything else is about making replay fast.

Insight 2: you only need a CRDT when there's concurrency

Here's the observation the whole algorithm rests on.

When you type locally, your edit's parent is the current state of the document. When a remote edit arrives that was made after everything you already have, its parent is also the current state. In both cases, there's nothing to transform. The edit's index is already correct, and you can apply it directly to a plain string.

Transformation is only needed when concurrent events meet. And in most real editing histories, concurrency is rare. Authors take turns, or there's only one author.

So Eg-walker keeps three things per replica:

  1. The event graph, on disk.
  2. The document, as plain text, in memory. No metadata at all.
  3. An internal CRDT state, which is temporary. It's built only to merge concurrent edits and then discarded. It's never saved to disk and never sent over the network.

Most of the time, the third item doesn't exist.

How replay works

When concurrent events do need merging, Eg-walker walks the event graph in topological order and builds its temporary CRDT as it goes. The clever part is that the CRDT tracks the document at two versions at once:

  • The effect version: the document with every event processed so far applied. This only moves forward.
  • The prepare version: the document exactly as the author of the current event saw it. This moves backward and forward.

Why two versions? Because an event like Delete(1) means "delete whatever was at index 1 in the author's view." To find the right character, you need the author's view (prepare). To know where that character sits in the real merged document, you need the full view (effect).

Each character gets one record in a list, including deleted ones. Each record holds two small states:

  • Prepare state: NotInsertedYet, Ins, or Del n (deleted by n concurrent deletions in the prepare view).
  • Effect state: Ins or Del.

And three operations move things around:

  • apply(e): interpret e in the prepare version, update both versions, and output the transformed operation for the real document.
  • retreat(e): make the prepare version behave as if e never happened.
  • advance(e): make e take effect in the prepare version again.

A walkthrough

Let's use the paper's own example. The document starts as hi. One user changes it to hey. At the same time, another user capitalizes it to Hi. After syncing, someone adds !.

Event Operation Branch
e1, e2 Insert h, Insert i shared start: hi
e3, e4 Insert(0, H), Delete(1) user B: Hi
e5, e6, e7 Delete(1), Insert(1, e), Insert(2, y) user A: hey
e8 Insert(3, !), parents: e4 and e7 after merging

Replaying in order:

  1. Apply e1 to e4. Each event's parent is the previous one, so nothing to adjust. The internal records are H, h (deleted), i, and the real document is Hi.
  2. Before e5, retreat e4 and e3. User A never saw B's edits, so the prepare version must forget them. H becomes NotInsertedYet, and h becomes Ins again. The effect state doesn't change: the real document is still Hi.
  3. Apply e5, e6, e7. A's Delete(1) is interpreted against A's view, hi, so it deletes i. A's inserts land after h in the record list. But when converted to the effect version, they're counted relative to the real document, which contains H. The real document becomes Hey.
  4. Before e8, advance e3 and e4. e8's author had seen both branches, so B's edits are brought back into the prepare view.
  5. Apply e8. Insert(3, "!") is interpreted against Hey, and the result is Hey!.

Notice what happened in step 3. A's Delete(1) was index-based, written against a document that never existed on B's machine. Retreating and advancing let the algorithm reconstruct exactly the view A had, at the cost of a few state flips.

A toy implementation

Here's a deliberately simple version in JavaScript, about 80 lines for the core. It skips all the performance work (more on that below), but it follows the algorithm's structure: topological sort, prepare/effect states, retreat/advance, and transformed output.

const NOT_INSERTED = -1, INS = 0; // sp: -1 not yet inserted, 0 inserted, n>0 deleted n times

export class EventGraph {
  constructor() { this.events = new Map(); }
  add(e) { this.events.set(e.id, e); return e; }

  // Lamport timestamp: one more than the max of the parents
  lamport(id) {
    const e = this.events.get(id);
    if (e._lt === undefined) e._lt = 1 + Math.max(0, ...e.parents.map(p => this.lamport(p)));
    return e._lt;
  }

  ancestors(ids) { // a version plus everything that happened before it
    const out = new Set(), stack = [...ids];
    while (stack.length) {
      const id = stack.pop();
      if (out.has(id)) continue;
      out.add(id);
      stack.push(...this.events.get(id).parents);
    }
    return out;
  }

  topoSort(shuffle = false) {
    const children = new Map(), order = [], seen = new Set();
    for (const e of this.events.values()) {
      for (const p of e.parents) {
        if (!children.has(p)) children.set(p, []);
        children.get(p).push(e.id);
      }
    }
    const visit = (id) => {
      if (seen.has(id)) return;
      if (!this.events.get(id).parents.every(p => seen.has(p))) return;
      seen.add(id); order.push(id);
      const kids = [...(children.get(id) || [])];
      if (shuffle) kids.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
      for (const k of kids) visit(k);
    };
    const roots = [...this.events.values()].filter(e => e.parents.length === 0).map(e => e.id);
    if (shuffle) roots.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
    for (const r of roots) visit(r);
    return order;
  }
}

export function replay(graph, { shuffle = false } = {}) {
  const order = graph.topoSort(shuffle);
  const pos = new Map(order.map((id, i) => [id, i]));
  const records = [];       // temporary CRDT: one record per character, incl. tombstones
  const target = new Map(); // event id -> record it touched
  let prepare = [];         // current prepare version
  let doc = '';             // the real document (effect version)

  const cmp = (a, b) =>     // total order on events: Lamport timestamp, then agent
    graph.lamport(a) - graph.lamport(b) ||
    (graph.events.get(a).agent < graph.events.get(b).agent ? -1 : 1);

  const nthVisibleInPrepare = (n) => {
    let seen = -1;
    for (let i = 0; i < records.length; i++)
      if (records[i].sp === INS && ++seen === n) return i;
    return -1;
  };
  const effectIndex = (recIdx) =>
    records.slice(0, recIdx).filter(r => r.se === INS).length;

  for (const id of order) {
    const e = graph.events.get(id);

    // 1. Move the prepare version to e.parents
    const oldSet = graph.ancestors(prepare), newSet = graph.ancestors(e.parents);
    const toRetreat = [...oldSet].filter(x => !newSet.has(x)).sort((a, b) => pos.get(b) - pos.get(a));
    const toAdvance = [...newSet].filter(x => !oldSet.has(x)).sort((a, b) => pos.get(a) - pos.get(b));
    for (const x of toRetreat) {
      const r = target.get(x);
      r.sp = graph.events.get(x).type === 'ins' ? NOT_INSERTED : r.sp - 1;
    }
    for (const x of toAdvance) {
      const r = target.get(x);
      r.sp = graph.events.get(x).type === 'ins' ? INS : r.sp + 1;
    }

    // 2. Apply e, interpreting its index in the prepare version
    if (e.type === 'ins') {
      let i = e.index === 0 ? 0 : nthVisibleInPrepare(e.index - 1) + 1;
      // Tie-break among concurrent inserts at the same spot (RGA-style rule)
      while (i < records.length && records[i].sp === NOT_INSERTED && cmp(records[i].id, id) > 0) i++;
      const rec = { id, ch: e.ch, sp: INS, se: INS };
      records.splice(i, 0, rec);
      target.set(id, rec);
      const at = effectIndex(i);
      doc = doc.slice(0, at) + e.ch + doc.slice(at);   // transformed op: insert at `at`
    } else {
      const i = nthVisibleInPrepare(e.index);
      const rec = records[i];
      target.set(id, rec);
      rec.sp += 1;
      if (rec.se === INS) {
        const at = effectIndex(i);
        rec.se = 'del';
        doc = doc.slice(0, at) + doc.slice(at + 1);    // transformed op: delete at `at`
      }                                                // already deleted elsewhere: no-op
    }
    prepare = [id];
  }
  return doc;
}

And a tiny helper to record edits the way a real editor would, with each event's parents set to whatever its author had seen:

export function makeAgent(graph, name) {
  let seq = 0, frontier = [];
  return {
    get frontier() { return frontier; },
    set frontier(f) { frontier = f; },
    ins(index, ch) {
      const e = graph.add({ id: `${name}${++seq}`, agent: name, type: 'ins', index, ch, parents: frontier });
      frontier = [e.id];
    },
    del(index) {
      const e = graph.add({ id: `${name}${++seq}`, agent: name, type: 'del', index, parents: frontier });
      frontier = [e.id];
    },
  };
}

Now replay the walkthrough:

const g = new EventGraph();
const a = makeAgent(g, 'a'), b = makeAgent(g, 'b');

a.ins(0, 'h'); a.ins(1, 'i');           // shared start: "hi"
b.frontier = a.frontier;

b.ins(0, 'H'); b.del(1);                // B: "Hi"
a.del(1); a.ins(1, 'e'); a.ins(2, 'y'); // A: "hey"

a.frontier = [...b.frontier, ...a.frontier]; // A syncs with B
a.ins(3, '!');

console.log(replay(g)); // "Hey!"

Every operation in the graph is stored exactly as typed. replay produces Hey!. Run it with { shuffle: true } and you get a different traversal order but the same result.

Two honest caveats about this toy. It uses a simple RGA-style rule to order concurrent insertions at the same position, while the authors use a variant of the Yjs algorithm designed to avoid interleaving concurrent runs of text. And it replays everything from scratch with linear scans, which brings us to the part that makes the real thing fast.

Insight 3: critical versions let you forget

A critical version is a point in the history where everything before it happened before everything after it. No branch crosses it. In a linear editing session, every single version is critical.

The paper's key observation is that critical versions split the history into independent sections. Events before one can't affect how events after it are transformed. That enables two optimizations:

  • Whenever replay reaches a critical version, the entire internal state can be thrown away. It's replaced with a single placeholder record meaning "some unknown text is here."
  • If an event and its parent are both critical, it's emitted unchanged. No CRDT work at all.

So when a concurrent edit arrives later, Eg-walker doesn't replay from the beginning of time. It finds the most recent critical version before the concurrency, starts from a placeholder, replays only the events since then, and applies the new ones.

For a document that's mostly edited by one person at a time, that means almost the entire history is skipped.

What the benchmarks show

The authors tested on real editing traces: sequential writing, real-time collaboration, and histories reconstructed from Git repositories. They compared their Rust implementation against Automerge, Yjs, their own optimized reference CRDT, and an OT implementation.

  • Merging long branches: On the Git Makefile trace, OT took an hour while Eg-walker took 24 ms, about 160,000 times faster.
  • Sequential editing: Eg-walker was 7 to 10 times faster than their reference CRDT, which itself outperformed both Yjs and Automerge.
  • Memory: In the steady state, while a document is open for editing, Eg-walker used 1 to 2 orders of magnitude less memory than the best CRDT.
  • Loading: Like OT, a document loads as plain text, orders of magnitude faster than the CRDTs tested.

The trade-offs

It isn't free, and the paper is upfront about where it costs.

Peak memory during a merge is CRDT-sized. While merging, Eg-walker's peak memory is roughly comparable to a CRDT's steady state. It's only cheap between merges.

Heavily concurrent histories gain little. On traces with constant concurrency, merge time was similar to their reference CRDT, because there are few critical versions to exploit. One trace had none at all.

Traversal order matters. On highly concurrent histories, a poorly chosen topological order made merging up to 8 times slower. The real implementation uses a heuristic to avoid that.

The worst case is O(n² log n). The authors note it's unlikely in real editing histories, but it exists.

You still store history. The event graph must be kept as long as concurrent edits might still arrive. It compresses well, but it's a cost.

It's plain text, for now. The paper covers plain text only, and the authors believe the approach can extend to rich text and other formats. That's not trivial: the team behind the Loro library, which draws on Eg-walker's ideas, has written that the original Peritext rich-text algorithm couldn't be used on top of it directly.

Why it matters

For years, the practical advice was: if you want lightweight, fast-loading documents, use OT and a central server. If you want offline editing and peer-to-peer sync, use a CRDT and pay for it in memory.

Eg-walker suggests that was a false choice. Keep the immutable history, keep the document as plain text, and build the CRDT only for the moment you actually need it.

If you want to dig deeper, the authors' production Rust implementation lives in Diamond Types, and there's a TypeScript reference implementation written for readability. The paper itself is very readable too.

I'm curious whether anyone here has run into the OT vs. CRDT trade-off in production. Which side did you pick, and would something like this have changed your decision?

articles.body_html:
A new pull request arrives.

GitHub Actions starts a workflow. The tests pass. Everything looks normal.

But a workflow can do more than run tests. Depending on its configuration, it may have access to repository secrets, a GitHub token, and other resources.

If that workflow executes code supplied by an untrusted contributor, a pull request can become a security problem before anyone merges it.

Here’s what every developer using GitHub Actions should check.

1. Understand the risky combination

The problem is not simply receiving a pull request.

The dangerous combination is:

  1. A workflow runs with elevated access.
  2. It checks out code from an untrusted pull request.
  3. It executes that code.

That code might run through a test command, a build script, a dependency installation, or a configuration file.

GitHub specifically warns about checking out and executing untrusted pull request code in privileged pull_request_target and workflow_run workflows.

2. Look closely at pull_request_target

pull_request_target can be useful for tasks such as labeling or commenting on a pull request.

But it runs in a privileged context associated with the base repository.

A risky pattern looks like this:

# Insecure example: do not copy
on: pull_request_target

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

      - run: make test

The checkout retrieves the pull request’s code.

The next step executes its Makefile.

If that file was changed by an attacker, the commands run in the workflow’s context. GitHub documents this pattern and its risks.

Checking out code and executing code are different steps. The risk appears when untrusted code is run with privileges it shouldn’t have.

For ordinary pull request tests, consider using the pull_request event with minimal permissions. Check your repository’s settings and event behavior, especially when working with forks.

3. Treat pull request text as untrusted too

Code isn’t the only input a contributor controls.

A pull request title, description, branch name, or comment may also be untrusted.

Consider this pattern:

# Risky: the title is inserted directly into a shell script
- run: |
    title="${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
    echo "$title"

GitHub evaluates the expression before the shell script runs. An unexpected title can change the generated script.

A safer pattern is to pass the value through an environment variable:

- name: Print the pull request title
  env:
    PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: |
    printf '%s\n' "$PR_TITLE"

The value is now handled as data by the shell in this example. Still avoid using it in eval or another command that interprets its contents as code.

GitHub’s security guidance recommends this intermediate-variable approach for inline scripts.

4. Give workflows only the permissions they need

Does a test job need permission to write to your repository?

If it only needs to read code, start with limited permissions:

permissions:
  contents: read

Then grant additional permissions only to jobs that require them.

Also review which secrets each job receives. A workflow that doesn’t need a deployment credential shouldn’t have access to one.

Smaller permissions reduce the impact if something goes wrong.

5. Check third-party actions

An action in your workflow is code that runs as part of your CI process.

Review what it does and what access its job has. For stronger protection against a tag being changed, GitHub recommends pinning third-party actions to a full commit SHA and verifying that the SHA belongs to the expected repository.

Also keep pinned actions updated through a deliberate review process. Pinning an old vulnerable version doesn’t make it safe.

6. Don’t assume masked logs protect secrets

GitHub can redact known secrets from logs. That helps prevent accidental exposure.

But log masking is not a security boundary. Malicious code with access to a secret may send it elsewhere rather than simply print it.

The stronger question is:

“Does this job need access to the secret at all?”

GitHub makes the same distinction in its guidance on compromised runners.

7. Review your workflows today

Open your repository’s .github/workflows directory and check:

  • Which workflows use pull_request_target or workflow_run?
  • Do privileged jobs check out and run pull request code?
  • Can untrusted text become part of a shell script?
  • Which jobs have write permissions?
  • Which jobs receive secrets?
  • Are third-party actions reviewed and pinned?
  • Does untrusted code run on a persistent self-hosted runner?

If you find a questionable workflow, trace what it actually executes—including scripts and dependencies—not just the YAML file.

The question behind the green check

A green CI badge tells you that the checks reported success.

It doesn’t tell you whether the workflow had the right permissions or safely handled untrusted input.

Before approving your next pull request, ask:

“What can this workflow execute—and what can that code access?”

That question can reveal problems a passing test suite never will.

Have you reviewed the permissions and triggers in your GitHub Actions workflows recently?

Further reading:

  • GitHub: Secure use of GitHub Actions
  • GitHub: Securely using pull_request_target
  • GitHub: Script injection in workflows
