articles.title: I tested my browser-based email checkers against dkimpy, checkdmarc and pyspf: 12,618 results, 76 disagreements
articles.description: Five email security tools that run in the browser (DKIM, DMARC, SPF, MX and header analysis), each benchmarked against the Python library people already trust. Where we disagreed, who was right, and the bug the benchmark caught.
articles.body_html:
I built five email security tools for Toggle9 that run in the browser: a DKIM checker, a DMARC checker, an SPF checker, an MX lookup and an email header analyzer. There's no backend. DNS queries go from your browser to Cloudflare's public resolver, and DKIM signatures are verified with WebCrypto.

That raises an obvious question: why would anyone trust a JavaScript reimplementation of RFC 6376? There are established open-source libraries for all of this: dkimpy for DKIM, checkdmarc for DMARC and MX, pyspf (the reference implementation of RFC 7208) for SPF, and mail-parser for headers.

So I ran each tool against one of them, on real data, and read every result where they disagreed.

The scoreboard

Tool Reference Test set Compared Same answer
DKIM checker dkimpy 1.1.8 510 real emails from 18 public mailing lists 623 signatures 623
Email header analyzer mail-parser 4.8.0 The same 510 emails 2,333 hops 2,333
DMARC checker checkdmarc 5.17.2 747 popular domains (Tranco top 500 + top 250 .uk) 705 domains 692 (98.2%)
SPF checker pyspf 2.0.14 The first 200 of those domains that publish SPF 454 IP checks 451
MX lookup checkdmarc 5.17.2 746 domains 8,503 checks 8,443

That's 12,618 results and 76 disagreements. The benchmarks ran on 22 and 23 October 2026. The rest of this post is about those 76.

How a browser does DNS

Every tool here needs DNS: TXT records for SPF, DMARC and DKIM keys, MX records, and TLSA and PTR records. Browsers can't send raw DNS queries, but they can use DNS over HTTPS. Cloudflare's resolver answers JSON:

const r = await fetch(`https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=${encodeURIComponent(name)}&type=${type}`, {
  headers: { accept: 'application/dns-json' },
  referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer',
  credentials: 'omit',
});
const j = await r.json();
// j.Status: 0 = NOERROR, 3 = NXDOMAIN. j.Answer: [{ name, type, TTL, data }]

The real resolver adds a cache per check, a limit of six queries in flight, a 6-second timeout and one retry. An SPF check can fan out into dozens of lookups, so the cache matters more than you'd expect.

For DMARC, SPF and MX, my tools and the reference libraries queried the same resolver (1.1.1.1), so a difference can't be blamed on two resolvers seeing different DNS.

DKIM: 623 of 623, and why 65 signatures "failed"

DKIM verification is canonicalization (RFC 6376 section 3.4), then a hash, then a signature check. The relaxed header rule fits in a few lines:

export function canonHeader(raw, how) {
  if (how === 'simple') return raw + '\r\n';
  const i = raw.indexOf(':');
  const name = raw.slice(0, i).replace(/[ \t]+$/, '').toLowerCase();
  const val = raw.slice(i + 1).replace(/\r\n(?=[ \t])/g, '').replace(/[ \t]+/g, ' ').replace(/^ | $/g, '');
  return `${name}:${val}\r\n`;
}

WebCrypto handles both DKIM signing algorithms, RSA and Ed25519 (simplified):

if (alg === 'ed25519-sha256')
  return crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', pubKey, { name: 'Ed25519' }, false, ['verify']);
return crypto.subtle.importKey('spki', spki, { name: 'RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5', hash: 'SHA-256' }, false, ['verify']);

The test set was 510 recent posts to 18 public mailing lists, taken from lore.kernel.org's public git mirrors. They had 623 signatures from 57 domains; two of the signatures used Ed25519. dkimpy and my checker gave the same pass or fail on all 623.

The useful part was the 65 signatures that failed in both. A checker that just says "fail" isn't much help, so mine reads the receiving server's own Authentication-Results header (RFC 8601) to work out when the email changed:

  • 62 had passed when the email arrived, according to the receiving server. They were changed afterwards. In 60 of them, a signed List-Unsubscribe header was missing: the archive removes it before it publishes the email.
  • 3 had already failed on arrival. They were changed on the way.

So most of the "broken DKIM" in that set wasn't broken at delivery. It's what an archive does to an email. That's the line the tool shows: "The email was fine when it was delivered."

Email headers: 2,333 of 2,333

The header analyzer turns Received: headers into a route: which server handed the email to which, when, and how long each hop took. mail-parser parses the same headers. On the same 510 emails, both found the same number of hops in every email, and all 2,333 hops matched on server, time and delay.

DMARC: the benchmark caught my bug

The first DMARC run agreed on everything for 682 of 705 domains (96.7%). I read every difference, and the biggest group was mine to fix.

My checker called it an error when an SPF record reached the same include: from two branches. msn.com, doi.org, grammarly.com and 7 others do this. I'd treated a repeat as a loop. Nothing in RFC 7208 makes a repeated include an error. Real loops get caught by the 10-lookup limit, and a repeat just counts against that limit. The fix: follow the repeat, count it again, and show a warning.

The second run agreed on 692 of 705 (98.2%). I read the 13 that were left by hand, against the RFCs:

Domains What happened Who's right
www.gov.uk, legislation.gov.uk, account.gov.uk, data.gov.uk No DMARC record of their own. The parent gov.uk record's sp=none applies to subdomains (RFC 9989). Mine
gcdn.co, thomsonreuters.co.uk SPF includes a name that doesn't exist in DNS, which is a permerror (RFC 7208 section 5.2) Mine
weather.com An unrelated TXT record at _dmarc alongside the real one; checkdmarc rejects it Mine
autodesk.com An = in the local part of a ruf address, which the standard allows Mine
alibabadns.com v=SPF1 in capitals. The ABNF is case-insensitive. Mine
globo.com rua=mailto: dmarc@… with a space. Both call the address invalid; checkdmarc then rejects the whole record, but RFC 9989 keeps p=none. Mine
iiko.it, who.int 15 and 17 DNS lookups (iiko.it confirmed by hand through 1.1.1.1). checkdmarc stops counting early. Mine
ozon.ru checkdmarc timed out Neither

"Mine" is my reading of the standards, written up with the RFC section each time. You don't have to take my word for it: the domains are real, so you can check them.

None of this makes checkdmarc a bad library. Rejecting a record the standards would accept is a reasonable choice for a tool that audits your own domain. Mine follows the standards' wording, because its job is to explain what a receiver should do with the record.

SPF: 451 of 454, and the 3 that weren't real

For each of 200 domains, I tested up to four IP addresses: the domain's own mail server, an address inside a range its record lists, an address reserved for documentation that never sends email, and a Google sending address for domains that include Google.

Three results differed: youtube.com, archive.org and youtube-nocookie.com, all for the same Google address. Large providers' DNS answers rotate, so an address can be listed in one lookup and missing from the next. Run again side by side, both tools agreed on all three.

MX: 8,443 of 8,503, and the rotation problem

The MX lookup checks a lot per domain: the MX hosts, their addresses, reverse DNS (PTR) and whether it points back, TLSA (DANE) records, MTA-STS and TLS reporting. Across 746 domains that came to 8,503 comparisons.

MX host sets matched on all 746 domains. MTA-STS and TLS reporting matched on all 746 too.

The addresses were the hard part. 738 of the 1,246 mail servers answered with a different few of their addresses each time. Google, Microsoft and Proofpoint spread their load that way, so two lookups a few minutes apart rarely agree, from any tool. Comparing those sets directly would only measure luck.

So the benchmark asks each server again over a few seconds. If those lookups turn up every address either tool saw, the server counts as rotating and isn't compared. That left 508 servers with steady answers, and 458 matched exactly. Of the 50 that didn't, 47 are Google or Proofpoint servers of the same rotating kind, whose other address didn't turn up in those few seconds.

The remaining 10 were differences in records. On 26 October I checked each one by hand through 1.1.1.1. In every case, the record my tool found is there:

  • TLSA: mx.ietf.org, two comcast.net servers and cm.com's Microsoft server publish TLSA records. checkdmarc reported none.
  • PTR: three servers (nic.ru, debian.org, ebi.ac.uk) have reverse DNS. checkdmarc reported none.
  • Forward-confirmed PTR: two huawei.com names do resolve back to their addresses.
  • Addresses: one Outlook server has IPv6 addresses that checkdmarc didn't list.

What I'd tell anyone writing a benchmark like this

  1. A reference library is a witness, not a judge. If you count disagreements as your failures, you end up copying the library's choices. Read each one against the spec.
  2. Read every difference, especially at the start. My first DMARC run had a real bug hiding behind a 96.7% score that looked fine.
  3. Handle rotating answers before comparing. Otherwise you're measuring DNS load balancing, not your code.
  4. Tie the results to the code. Each tool's test file hashes its engine and compares that with the hash stored in its benchmark result. Change the DKIM verifier without re-running the benchmark, and npm test fails: 
test('dkim-bench.json was made by the engine that ships', () => {
  const b = JSON.parse(readFileSync(new URL('dkim-bench.json', dir), 'utf8'));
  const h = createHash('sha256')
    .update(readFileSync(new URL('verify.js', dir)))
    .update(readFileSync(new URL('compute.js', dir)))
    .digest('hex').slice(0, 16);
  assert.equal(b.engine, h);
});

So the numbers quoted on each tool's page can't silently drift away from the code.

Try them

All five run in your browser, with no account. When you check a domain, only the DNS names go to Cloudflare's public resolver. Headers and emails you paste are read on your device.

  • DKIM checker
  • DMARC checker
  • SPF checker
  • MX lookup
  • Email header analyzer

If you check DMARC for a living, I'd like to hear where you think I've read RFC 9989 wrong, especially on those 13.

articles.title: I got tired of reading CSS bugs in a tiny overlay, so I made my debugger print a report
articles.description: BeeLadybug, my open-source debug overlay, has always shown what's happening in real time: FPS, logs,...
articles.body_html:
BeeLadybug, my open-source debug overlay, has always shown what's happening in real time: FPS, logs, !important, z-index traps, clicks being swallowed by the wrong element.

The problem is the overlay. Make it big and it covers the game or the page you're debugging. Make it small, the way it is now, and you're squinting at a phone-sized box on the left of the screen while the rows scroll past.

One evening I gave up and asked myself a simple question: why can't I just press a key and get everything on one page, to read calmly?

One key, one file

Version 0.6.1 adds exportReport(). Press F8, or the EXPORT button, and you get report-YYYYMMDD-HHMM.html:

  • a summary at the top: errors, warnings, ok
  • the Core log with sim time and frame
  • series: FPS min / avg / max, nodes, mutations
  • one section per adapter: Canvas hitboxes and collisions, DOM box model and clipped nodes, CSS (!important, stacking contexts, intercepted clicks, overflow), long tasks, slow resources, Python metrics

It's plain HTML with a dark theme. Ctrl+P turns it into a PDF. You can also get json (for CI or an AI agent) or csv (for a spreadsheet).

import { BeeLadybugCore, exportReport } from 'bee-ladybug';

const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
// ...attach adapters...
exportReport(bee, { format: 'html' }); // downloads the file

In headless mode (ui: false) nothing is downloaded. The function just returns the data, so it works in Node and in bots too.

How it fits a "blind" Core

The Core still knows nothing about Canvas, the DOM or Python. Each adapter can now register an optional snapshot() hook that returns rows like { severity, selector, rule, value, source }. The exporter asks every registered adapter for its snapshot, and if one throws, it becomes a single warn row while the rest of the report still renders. A new adapter only has to implement snapshot() to show up in the report.

Then I pointed it at real sites

First, my own games portal. It found:

  • my .entry-content creating a stacking context that traps the z-index of the game grid
  • a container blocking clicks on three elements
  • an average of 33 FPS, which explains a lot

Then, for fun, a big professional games portal. 25 errors, 51 warnings 😄 To be fair, most of them are intentional tricks: negative margins so a carousel can bleed to the edges, and content clipped on purpose inside cards. Their site works great. It still averaged ~52 FPS with 3× my DOM nodes, which taught me more than the error count did.

…and it found bugs in itself

The best part of testing on real pages: the report exposed its own weak spots.

  • an icon from the WordPress admin bar slipped through the filter
  • the same row repeated dozens of times instead of being grouped as ×N
  • the summary said "0 errors" while the log had four of them

All three are being fixed. A debugger that finds bugs in itself on its first real run felt like a good sign.

Try it

Install it in your project:

npm i bee-ladybug

Or try it right now without installing: open any page, press F12 and paste this in the console, then press F8 for the report.

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.6.1/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Feedback welcome, especially from people debugging Canvas games and DOM-heavy pages.

articles.title: Percent-Encoding: The Reserved Characters That Break URLs
articles.description: Reserved means the character has a job in that position. Leave it unencoded in a value and it splits your data into parameters or fragments, with no error.
articles.body_html:
A URL is not a string with escapes in it. It is a small grammar with several interchangeable parts — scheme, authority, path, query, fragment — and a character's meaning depends on which part it appears in. Percent-encoding exists so that data can be carried inside those parts without being mistaken for the grammar itself. When that goes wrong, nothing reports an error: the value simply arrives shorter, split in two, or pointing somewhere the server never sees.

The two sets, and one detail about them

RFC 3986 divides characters into two groups.

Unreserved — A–Z, a–z, 0–9, -, ., _, ~. These never need encoding, and encoding them anyway creates a second spelling of the same URL. That looks harmless until two spellings reach a cache, a signature calculation or a URL-based access rule, and are treated as two different resources.

Reserved, in two flavours:

  • gen-delims — :, /, ?, #, [, ], @
  • sub-delims — !, $, &, ', (, ), *, +, ,, ;, =

Reserved does not mean "always encode". It means "this character has a job here". : is a delimiter in the authority (host:port) and perfectly ordinary data in a path segment. & is a separator between query parameters and perfectly ordinary data inside a path. The rule is always relative to the component you are writing.

One detail that trips parsers: percent-encoded triplets are case-insensitive — %2F and %2f mean the same octet — but string equality in your code is not. Canonicalise to uppercase hex before comparing, hashing or signing, or two identical URLs will produce two different signatures.

The characters that cause incidents

& in a query value. The value ends at the &; everything after it becomes another parameter. Symptom: a long token arrives truncated at an arbitrary point, and an extra parameter appears in the request that no client intended to send.

# anywhere in a query value. Everything from the # onward becomes the fragment, and a browser never sends the fragment to the server. So the server sees the value cut at that point, and the browser's own address bar shows the rest — the single most confusing version of this bug, because the URL looks complete to everyone who inspects it locally.

+ in a query value. Under application/x-www-form-urlencoded rules it means a space, so C++ becomes C. In a path it is a literal plus. Send a literal plus as %2B if you want it to survive being handled by two different libraries.

% on its own. A literal percent sign must be %25. A single % followed by something that is not two hex digits makes the URL invalid, and strict parsers reject the whole thing rather than the character — which is why an input like 100% or %AB in a template can break an otherwise fine request.

Space. %20 in a path and in a standards-compliant query; + in form-encoded data. Both are widely accepted on the way in, and that mutual tolerance is precisely why the bug survives so long: it works with the parser you tested and fails with the one in production.

/ inside a path segment value. Encode it as %2F and the value no longer looks like two segments — but many servers decode the path before routing, so %2F is turned back into a separator and your value splits anyway. Some servers reject encoded slashes outright, and the reason is security: %2F and %2E are the building blocks of path traversal attempts, so proxies and application servers have strong opinions about them. The honest conclusion is that a value containing a slash does not belong in a single path segment.

? in a query value. Legal in a query by the grammar, and best encoded anyway, since a second ? invites a second round of parsing in intermediaries.

Non-ASCII is bytes, not characters

This is where percent-encoding stops looking like an escaping scheme and starts looking like an encoding.

A %XX triplet carries one byte, not one character. A character outside ASCII has to be turned into bytes first, and the only interoperable choice is UTF-8:

  • é is U+00E9, two bytes in UTF-8 (C3 A9), so it encodes to %C3%A9.
  • A CJK character such as U+4E2D is three bytes (E4 B8 AD), so it encodes to %E4%B8%AD — nine characters to carry one.

If the producer used a different legacy encoding, the triplets are still perfectly well-formed and still decode to something — just not to the text that was sent. A GBK-encoded Chinese string arriving at a UTF-8 decoder produces a page of replacement characters, and nothing in the request looks wrong. So "the encoding is valid" and "the characters are correct" are separate questions, and the second one needs the producer's encoding to be known.

The related rule for implementers: always percent-encode bytes, never code points and never characters. In languages where a string is a sequence of UTF-16 code units, encoding a character directly is how astral-plane characters get written as surrogate halves, which no decoder will accept.

A decoder should refuse, not guess

Decoding is where the damage becomes permanent, because a decoder that is generous with invalid input turns a visible bug into a plausible value.

  • An incomplete triplet at the end of the input (%E4%B8) is invalid. Truncating it silently produces text that is almost right.
  • An invalid UTF-8 byte sequence must be an error. Substituting U+FFFD without saying so means the caller never learns that the sender used the wrong encoding — and a value with a replacement character in it can be stored, indexed and passed along for years.
  • Over-long encodings — the historical trick of writing / as %C0%AF — must be rejected rather than decoded to the shorter form, since that is precisely what makes them dangerous in a security context.
  • A % that is not followed by two hex digits is a malformed URL. Reporting it as malformed is more useful than treating % as literal, because the caller then finds the template that forgot to escape.

A decoder that does the opposite — normalising, repairing and reporting success — is the reason two systems can disagree about the same URL while both claim to have decoded it. The strict-but-explicit behaviour is what the URL encoder and decoder implements: it shows which characters it changed, keeps UTF-8 byte handling separate from the text, and points at the exact position of a malformed sequence instead of quietly dropping it.

The rules worth keeping

  1. Encode per component, not per URL. &, =, # and + are data in one part and syntax in another.
  2. Never decode twice. %2520 is a percent sign followed by 20, not a space; if a second decode "fixes" it, the producer double-encoded, and that is their bug to fix.
  3. Compare canonical forms: uppercase hex triplets, no needlessly encoded unreserved characters, one spelling per resource.
  4. Treat non-ASCII as UTF-8 bytes and say so explicitly; where the sender's encoding is unknown, ask rather than assume.
  5. Prefer refusing malformed input to repairing it — this is the difference between a decoder and a data corruption device.

The comparison with Base64 covers which of the two layers a given payload needs; when the payload is a token that must survive a query string untouched, the URL-safe alphabet is usually the better starting point than escaping your way out of an alphabet that already contains + and /.

articles.title: Email validation in JavaScript: test your signup rules with mailrules
articles.description: I was asked to add stronger email validation to our forms at work. Honestly, I thought we were...
articles.body_html:
I was asked to add stronger email validation to our forms at work. Honestly, I thought we were overcomplicating it at first.

Then I started looking into the details.

An email can have valid syntax and still come from a disposable provider. A signup form might need to reject certain domains, restrict access to a company, or flag shared addresses like support@. Someone typing gmial.com probably needs a helpful suggestion.

Those decisions depend on the application. I wanted a way to define them once, inspect the result, and reuse the same policy across projects.

That is what I have been building with mailrules, an MIT-licensed email validation library for JavaScript and TypeScript.

The latest addition is a live playground. You can enter an address, change the rules, see the decision, and copy the configuration into your project before installing anything.

Start with a small signup policy

mailrules uses validator.js for syntax checks and fakeout for its default disposable-domain data.

npm install mailrules

Here is a policy that rejects known disposable domains and a custom blocked domain, suggests possible typos, and warns about role addresses:

import { createEmailValidator } from 'mailrules';

const validator = createEmailValidator({
  blocklist: { domains: ['spam.example'] },
  suggestions: true,
  roleAccounts: 'warn',
});

validator.check('alice@example.com').valid;
// true

validator.check('hello@mailinator.com').reasons;
// ['disposable']

validator.check('person@spam.example').reasons;
// ['blocked']

validator.check('support@example.com').warnings?.[0]?.code;
// 'role_account' — a warning; the address is still accepted

validator.check('alex@gmial.com').suggestion;
// 'alex@gmail.com'

Suggestions are advisory. They never replace the submitted address or change whether it passes validation. A result can contain both a rejection and a suggestion; for example, the installed disposable dataset also flags gmial.com. If someone chooses the suggested address, validate that new value too.

See why an address was rejected

A boolean is useful for a form, but it does not explain which configuration entry caused a rejection. For that, there is explain():

const result = validator.explain('person@sub.spam.example');

result.reason;
// 'blocked'

result.matchedRule;
// {
//   source: 'blocklist',
//   type: 'domain',
//   value: 'spam.example',
//   matchedSubdomain: true
// }

Domain rules include subdomains by default. You can turn that off with includeSubdomains: false.

Allowlists also need predictable behavior: an explicit block always wins in mailrules. An allowlist can exempt an address from disposable rejection, but it does not override a blocklist entry. For an invitation-only or company-only form, allowlistMode: 'only' requires an allowlist match.

Try the policy before wiring it into a form

In the playground, you can edit domain and mailbox lists, switch role-address and free-provider policies, inspect the result, and copy JavaScript or React examples.

Role addresses and free providers each support classification, warnings, or blocking. Both checks are off by default. A provider-list non-match does not prove an address belongs to a business, and a Gmail address is not inherently a bad signup.

The playground also has a working React Hook Form + Zod example, so you can see how a policy affects field errors and normalized output. Validation happens locally in your browser; the playground does not send the entered address to a validation service.

Reuse it with Zod and React Hook Form

The optional Zod 4 adapter turns the same validator into a schema:

npm install mailrules zod

import { z } from 'zod';
import { zodEmail } from 'mailrules/zod';

// Reuse the validator from the first example.
const signupSchema = z.object({
  email: zodEmail(validator),
});

signupSchema.parse({ email: ' Alice@EXAMPLE.COM ' });
// { email: 'Alice@example.com' }

signupSchema.safeParse({ email: 'hello@mailinator.com' }).success;
// false

You can pass that schema to React Hook Form through zodResolver. The integration guide includes the full form example and a Standard Schema adapter for tools that support it.

Warnings remain successful schema results. Use check() or explain() when you want to display those warnings separately. Apply the policy on the backend accepting submissions as well, since browser checks can be bypassed.

React, Zod, and the playground are not required downloads for a normal mailrules installation. Install Zod when you use its adapter. The playground lives in the same repository but is excluded from the npm package.

There is also a CSV command

For reviewing an existing list with an email column:

npx mailrules --input contacts.csv --status rejected --output rejected.csv

This exports rejected rows with validation reasons. You can also export accepted rows or supply a JSON rules configuration. The CLI runs on Node.js 22.12 or newer and processes bounded files in memory; the guide documents its limits.

What “accepted” means here

mailrules checks syntax and your configured application rules locally, in a browser bundle or Node.js. It does not check DNS, MX records, or SMTP, and an accepted result does not establish that a mailbox exists or that the person submitting it owns it.

There are tools with a broader verification scope, including email-validator-js, which documents MX and SMTP checks and a hosted API. For this project, I wanted reusable local policies with clear explanations.

If you have dealt with messy signup forms, I would love to hear about a rule that was harder to get right than you expected. Especially cases where a strict rule ended up rejecting legitimate users.

  • Try the playground
  • Source code and documentation
  • Install from npm

articles.title: Build a 'days since' streak counter in React with localStorage (that survives midnight, DST and bad data)
articles.description: "Days since I last smoked." "Days since the last production incident." "Days without sugar." A streak...
articles.body_html:
"Days since I last smoked." "Days since the last production incident." "Days without sugar." A streak counter looks like the easiest widget in the world: store a start date and subtract. Then it shows 0 for two days after a clock change, crashes on the one user whose localStorage holds garbage, and stays on yesterday's number when the tab is left open overnight.

Here's the version I ended up with. It's plain JavaScript plus one React hook, with no libraries. All the logic below was run under Node 20 with TZ=Europe/Warsaw and TZ=America/New_York.

Rule 1: store calendar days, not timestamps

A streak is about days the user lived through, not milliseconds. If you store Date.now() and divide by 86,400,000, a 23-hour DST day or a trip across time zones will shift your count. So store a local day key, a plain YYYY-MM-DD string:

export function toDayKey(date = new Date()) {
  const y = date.getFullYear();
  const m = String(date.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, "0");
  const d = String(date.getDate()).padStart(2, "0");
  return `${y}-${m}-${d}`;
}

Note the use of getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are local, not toISOString(). toISOString() is UTC, so in Warsaw shortly after midnight it would still say yesterday.

Rule 2: subtract day keys in UTC

To count the days between two keys, turn each into a UTC midnight. UTC has no DST, so every day there really is 86,400,000 ms long and Math.round handles the rest:

export function daysBetweenKeys(a, b) {
  const [y1, m1, d1] = a.split("-").map(Number);
  const [y2, m2, d2] = b.split("-").map(Number);
  return Math.round(
    (Date.UTC(y2, m2 - 1, d2) - Date.UTC(y1, m1 - 1, d1)) / 86400000
  );
}

export function daysSince(startKey, todayKey = toDayKey()) {
  return Math.max(0, daysBetweenKeys(startKey, todayKey));
}

Quick checks that used to bite me:

daysBetweenKeys("2026-03-28", "2026-03-30"); // 2  (EU DST weekend)
daysBetweenKeys("2026-10-24", "2026-10-26"); // 2  (EU DST ends)
daysBetweenKeys("2024-02-28", "2024-03-01"); // 2  (leap year)
daysSince("2026-11-01", "2026-10-26");       // 0  (future start never goes negative)

Math.max(0, …) matters more than it looks. Users change their device clock, and a negative streak is a bug report waiting to happen.

Rule 3: resetting should keep the record

People like seeing their best streak, and it makes a reset feel less painful. A reset is a pure function that takes the old state and returns the new one:

export function reset(state, todayKey = toDayKey()) {
  const current = daysSince(state.startKey, todayKey);
  return {
    startKey: todayKey,
    best: Math.max(state.best ?? 0, current),
    resets: (state.resets ?? 0) + 1,
  };
}

reset({ startKey: "2026-10-01", best: 10, resets: 0 }, "2026-10-26");
// { startKey: "2026-10-26", best: 25, resets: 1 }

Because todayKey is a parameter, it's trivial to test without mocking Date.

Rule 4: treat localStorage as hostile

localStorage can be missing (some private modes), full, or hold an old format from last year's version of your app. Wrap it so that the worst case is "start fresh", never a white screen:

export function load(storage, key, todayKey = toDayKey()) {
  try {
    const raw = storage.getItem(key);
    if (!raw) return { startKey: todayKey, best: 0, resets: 0 };
    const s = JSON.parse(raw);
    if (!/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(s.startKey)) throw new Error("bad data");
    return { best: 0, resets: 0, ...s };
  } catch {
    return { startKey: todayKey, best: 0, resets: 0 };
  }
}

export function save(storage, key, state) {
  try {
    storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(state));
  } catch {
    // quota exceeded or storage disabled: keep working in memory
  }
}

Passing storage in, instead of touching window.localStorage directly, lets you test it in Node with a five-line fake:

const mem = new Map();
const storage = {
  getItem: (k) => mem.get(k) ?? null,
  setItem: (k, v) => mem.set(k, v),
};
mem.set("streak", "{oops");
load(storage, "streak", "2026-10-27").startKey; // "2026-10-27", no crash

If you ever change the shape, add a version field now. Future you will thank you.

Rule 5: tick over at local midnight

The classic bug: the tab stays open overnight and still shows yesterday's number. You don't need a one-second interval. Schedule a single timeout for the next local midnight, and also refresh when the tab becomes visible again, because timers get throttled in background tabs and laptops go to sleep.

import { useEffect, useState, useCallback } from "react";
import { toDayKey, daysSince, reset, load, save } from "./streak";

function msUntilNextMidnight(now = new Date()) {
  const next = new Date(now);
  next.setHours(24, 0, 0, 0); // local midnight, DST-aware
  return next - now;
}

function useToday() {
  const [today, setToday] = useState(toDayKey);
  useEffect(() => {
    let timer;
    const refresh = () => setToday(toDayKey());
    const schedule = () => {
      timer = setTimeout(() => { refresh(); schedule(); }, msUntilNextMidnight() + 1000);
    };
    schedule();
    document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", refresh);
    return () => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      document.removeEventListener("visibilitychange", refresh);
    };
  }, []);
  return today;
}

export function useStreak(key = "streak") {
  const today = useToday();
  const [state, setState] = useState(() =>
    typeof window === "undefined"
      ? { startKey: today, best: 0, resets: 0 }
      : load(window.localStorage, key, today)
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    save(window.localStorage, key, state);
  }, [key, state]);

  // keep several tabs in sync
  useEffect(() => {
    const onStorage = (e) => {
      if (e.key === key) setState(load(window.localStorage, key, toDayKey()));
    };
    window.addEventListener("storage", onStorage);
    return () => window.removeEventListener("storage", onStorage);
  }, [key]);

  const doReset = useCallback(() => setState((s) => reset(s, toDayKey())), []);

  return {
    days: daysSince(state.startKey, today),
    best: Math.max(state.best, daysSince(state.startKey, today)),
    resets: state.resets,
    reset: doReset,
  };
}

setHours(24, 0, 0, 0) asks the engine for "the next local midnight", so DST is handled for you. The extra second avoids landing at 23:59:59.999 because of timer jitter.

The component 

export function StreakCard({ label }) {
  const { days, best, reset } = useStreak(`streak:${label}`);
  return (
    <section aria-live="polite">
      <h2>{label}</h2>
      <p style={{ fontSize: "3rem", margin: 0 }}>{days}</p>
      <p>{days === 1 ? "day" : "days"} · best: {best}</p>
      <button onClick={() => confirm("Reset this streak?") && reset()}>
        Reset
      </button>
    </section>
  );
}

Two small UX details: aria-live so screen readers announce the new count at midnight, and a confirm step, because an accidental tap that wipes a 200-day streak is the fastest way to lose a user.

Server rendering note

If you render on the server (Next.js and friends), the server doesn't know the user's time zone or their localStorage. Render a neutral placeholder and fill in the number after hydration, or you'll get hydration mismatch warnings around midnight. The typeof window guard above covers the initial state.

Recap

  • Store local day keys (YYYY-MM-DD), not timestamps.
  • Subtract them in UTC, and clamp at zero.
  • Make reset a pure function that keeps the best streak.
  • Treat localStorage as unreliable: validate, catch and fall back.
  • Re-render at local midnight and on visibilitychange.

That's about 100 lines for a counter that behaves correctly on DST weekends, on leap days, and in tabs left open for a week.

If you'd rather not build it yourself, I made this into a free app with countdowns and "days since" trackers, no ads and no sign-up: CountMyDays.

articles.title: O fantasma que assombra o PDF da Fecombustíveis: um robô que transforma a tributação dos combustíveis em XML
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Transparência antes de tudo: este projeto usa o Google Gemini (API fechada) para ler o PDF — não um modelo open-weight. Conto abaixo por que fiz essa escolha, onde o código é aberto e o que falta para trocar por um modelo aberto.

What I Built

Todo mês, sem aviso de horário, aparece um PDF no site da Fecombustíveis: a "Carga tributária estadual" dos combustíveis. Ali estão o PMPF, a alíquota de ICMS, o tributo estadual e o federal de gasolina, diesel, etanol e GNV para as 27 UFs.

Quem emite nota fiscal de combustível no Brasil precisa desses números para a Lei da Transparência (o "valor aproximado dos tributos" no cupom). No nosso caso, eles alimentam o XML TransparenciaTributos usado no nosso sistema de emissão fiscal. Antes, alguém abria o PDF — com as tabelas em imagem — e digitava dezenas de valores à mão.

O Transparência de Tributos – Combustíveis é o "fantasma na máquina" que faz isso sozinho:

  • 👻 Assombra a página da Fecombustíveis a cada 8 horas procurando o PDF novo;
  • 📄 Lê o PDF com IA e devolve os valores por combustível e UF;
  • 🧮 Confere as contas (PMPF × alíquota = ICMS; no GNV, PMPF × 9,25% = PIS/COFINS) e se recusa a gravar se algo não fechar;
  • 🕯️ Honra o passado: o bloco de vigência antigo não é apagado — ele "termina" no dia anterior (ex.: até 30/09/2026) e nasce um bloco novo (01/10/2026 até 2050). O histórico de cada tributo fica preservado no XML;
  • 🔔 Avisa por e-mail e no Discord quando a tributação muda;
  • 🌐 Publica uma página pública com os tributos por estado.

Minha leitura do tema: o PDF mensal é um fantasma que aparece quando quer, e a ideia foi deixar a máquina vigiando por mim — sem perder a memória dos meses anteriores, que é o que o fisco pede quando confere uma nota antiga.

Demo

  • Gerador (passos 1–3): https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/
  • Tributos por estado: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/tributos.html

Fluxo no site:

  1. Passo 1 – o PDF mais recente já vem selecionado, com o XML do mês anterior como base.
  2. Passo 2 – a IA extrai os valores; o que mudou fica amarelo (com o valor antigo embaixo) e conta que não fecha ganha borda vermelha. Tudo é editável na tabela.
  3. Passo 3 – Gerar XML, Baixar XML e, se quiser, Baixar Excel.

Code

imextecnologia / tributacao

tributacao

Transparência de Tributos – Combustíveis

Site estático (GitHub Pages) que gera todo mês o XML TransparenciaTributos a partir do PDF "Carga tributária estadual" da Fecombustíveis.

Site: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/ · Tributos por estado: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/tributos.html

Como funciona

  1. Busca do PDF – a cada 8 horas um workflow procura o PDF novo na página da Fecombustíveis, salva em pdf/ e já gera o XML do mês em xml/ (veja Busca automática do PDF).
  2. Leitura com IA – o site envia o PDF ao Google Gemini, que devolve os valores por combustível e UF.
  3. Comparação – os valores são comparados com o XML do mês anterior (em xml/) e o que mudou fica destacado.
  4. Geração – para cada combustível que mudou, o bloco antigo termina no dia anterior (ex.: 30/09/2026) e é criado um bloco novo (ex.: 01/10/2026 até 01/01/2050). Combustíveis sem mudança ficam como estão Também é possível baixar uma planilha…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Sem servidor. É um site estático no GitHub Pages; tudo roda no navegador ou num job do GitHub Actions.

Busca automática (.github/workflows/buscar-pdf.yml, cron 0 */8 * * *):

  1. scripts/buscar-pdf.js lê a página da Fecombustíveis e pega o link do PDF mais recente pela data no nome ("10 OUTUBRO 2026" vem antes de "01 OUTUBRO 2026"). Se a página falhar, tenta o link no padrão do mês atual e do próximo.
  2. scripts/gerar-xml.js gera o XML do PDF novo usando o mesmo prompt, produtos e UFs do index.html — o script extrai essas constantes direto do HTML, então site e robô nunca divergem.
  3. scripts/buscar-painel.js relê o quadro oficial de percentuais e atualiza painel.json.
  4. Se algo mudou: commit, publicação do site e aviso por e-mail/Discord com o diff.

A IA. O PDF vai para o Gemini com um prompt que pede somente JSON num formato fixo (gasolina/diesel com valor único; etanol e GNV por UF). O site tenta uma lista de modelos em ordem (gemini-flash-latest → gemini-flash-lite-latest → gemini-2.5-flash → gemini-2.5-flash-lite), com nova tentativa em 429/503.

A rede de segurança importa mais que o modelo. IA lendo tabela em imagem erra dígito. Por isso:

// PMPF × alíquota precisa bater com o ICMS (etanol no MT usa base de 50%)
const base = (p.key === "etanol" && row.uf === "MT") ? row.pmpf * 0.5 : row.pmpf;
if (Math.abs(base * row.aliquota / 100 - row.estadual) > 0.0015) err.estadual = true;
// GNV: PIS/COFINS = PMPF × 9,25%
if (p.key === "gnv" && Math.abs(row.pmpf * 0.0925 - row.federal) > 0.0015) err.federal = true;

No Actions, se qualquer conta não fecha, o XML não é gravado — o aviso pede revisão humana no site, e as execuções seguintes tentam de novo. Uma alucinação nunca vira nota fiscal.

Economia de chamadas: se o XML do mês já existe em xml/, o site carrega direto; o resultado da IA fica salvo no navegador, então recarregar a página não chama o modelo de novo.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Sendo honesto: a parte de IA aqui não é aberta. Escolhi o Gemini porque o plano gratuito lê PDF com tabela em imagem de forma confiável, não exige cartão e o volume é mínimo (uma leitura por mês). Para um site estático sem servidor, isso resolveu.

Mas o projeto mostra exatamente onde um caminho fechado incomoda:

  • A chave fica exposta no index.html publicado (restrita por referenciador e API, mas ainda assim pública). Um modelo local não teria chave nenhuma.
  • Dependência de fornecedor: precisei de uma lista de fallbacks porque modelos somem ou mudam de nome. Um modelo open-weight com versão fixa daria a mesma resposta amanhã — algo valioso quando o resultado vai para documento fiscal.
  • Dados: no plano gratuito o Google pode usar o conteúdo enviado. Hoje só vai o PDF público da Fecombustíveis, então não há problema — mas eu não poderia fazer o mesmo com documentos de clientes.

O que é aberto: todo o código, o workflow, as regras de validação e o histórico de XMLs estão no GitHub, públicos. Qualquer posto, contador ou software fiscal pode copiar, auditar as contas ou usar os XMLs.

Próximo passo: como o prompt já pede JSON estrito e a validação aritmética independe do modelo, a troca é isolada numa função (chamarGemini). O plano é testar um modelo de visão open-weight (por exemplo, Gemma) rodando dentro do próprio GitHub Actions ou localmente e comparar a taxa de "contas que não fecham" com o Gemini.

The Spirit of It

No Día de los Muertos a gente lembra quem veio antes. No XML de tributos, nada é apagado: cada mês que passa vira um bloco com data de fim, e o novo começa no dia seguinte. Quando alguém abrir uma nota de setembro daqui a cinco anos, os valores de setembro ainda estarão lá.

E o fantasma? Ele aparece às 21h, 5h e 13h (horário de Brasília), olha a página, e na maioria das vezes vai embora em silêncio. Quando a tributação muda, ele deixa um recado no Discord. 👻

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot — a automação inteira (busca, geração do XML, publicação e avisos) roda em GitHub Actions.

articles.title: From client-only to SSR: building Gemkit, a SvelteKit-style framework for Web Components
articles.description: How I added SSR and hydration to the Gem Web Components library, built an app framework on Rsbuild, and benchmarked it against SvelteKit, Nuxt and Next.js.
articles.body_html:
A long time ago I built Gem, a library for building UI components and apps with Web Components. It was pleasant to use, but it had one big weakness: client-side rendering only. Even GemBook, its documentation site generator, rendered everything in the browser, so search engines saw an almost empty HTML page.

This post is about how I brought Gem to the server: first a gem-ssr prototype on jsdom that could serialize and hydrate, then moving away from jsdom and isolating requests, and finally Gemkit, an app framework inspired by Next.js and SvelteKit. At the end, I compare it with SvelteKit, Nuxt and Next.js using the RealWorld app.

Why SSR is hard for Web Components

React and Vue components are framework abstractions, so the server can turn a virtual DOM into a string. Web Components are different, they depend on the browser:

  • Elements are class extends HTMLElement, which needs customElements, HTMLElement, document...
  • Styles and content live in Shadow DOM, which plain HTML could not express
  • Gem templates are based on (a modified) lit-html, which renders real DOM nodes, not a virtual DOM

Fortunately, Declarative Shadow DOM is now supported by all major browsers: <template shadowrootmode="open"> puts Shadow DOM directly in HTML. The remaining question was how to run Gem elements in Node.js.

The prototype: serialization and hydration on jsdom

The most direct idea: Gem needs a DOM, so give it one. The first version of gem-ssr used jsdom to emulate the browser and got the core of SSR working:

1. Serialization. Elements are created and rendered on the server, then serialized to HTML together with their Shadow DOM, output as Declarative Shadow DOM. The browser can display the page right away.

2. Hydration. The server output contains comment markers for each template binding. When an element renders on the client for the first time, it uses the markers to connect bindings to the existing DOM. It only attaches event listeners and sets properties, it doesn't recreate the DOM. Templates also carry a digest; on a mismatch, the client warns and re-renders only that part.

That proved SSR with Web Components works. But jsdom was far from production ready:

  • jsdom is heavy, every request goes through a full DOM implementation
  • There is only one global document, location and history, so concurrent requests pollute each other

gem-ssr: dropping jsdom, isolating requests

Next, I moved gem-ssr towards production:

1. Render to strings without jsdom. gem-ssr provides only the minimal DOM Gem needs and compiles templates to strings on the server. The serialization and hydration protocol stays the same.

2. Request isolation. With AsyncLocalStorage, stores, history, location and the i18n language are scoped per request.

3. Streaming. render returns an async iterable. Content before pending async elements is sent first, and independent async elements are awaited in parallel:

import { render } from '@mantou/gem-ssr';

const stream = ReadableStream.from(render(html`<app-root></app-root>`, { url: req.url }));

At this point gem-ssr could run in a real server. But routing, data loading, forms and deployment still had to be assembled by every project. That's what Gemkit is for.

Gemkit: the app framework for Gem

Gemkit borrows heavily from Next.js and SvelteKit: file-based routing, layouts, load, form actions, SSR/SSG/ISR. It is an Rsbuild plugin, so Rsbuild's config, dev server and plugins all keep working.

npm create gemkit@latest my-app

One file is one page 

// src/pages/index.ts
@page('Home')
export default class HomePage extends GemElement {
  @template()
  #content = () => html`<h1>Hello Gemkit</h1>`;
}

No @customElement needed, the tag name comes from the file path, and Gem and common Gemkit APIs are auto-imported. This page is prerendered to dist/web/index.html at build time and hydrated on the client.

For Gemkit, unplugin-gem also got an ssr option: its swc plugin adds a key to module-level createStore calls based on the file path and variable name, so client and server builds agree. Stores updated during server rendering are output by key, and the client uses those values, so the first render matches the HTML.

The project structure will look familiar if you know SvelteKit:

src/
  app.ts               global styles, stores
  app.server.ts        handle: runs before each server request
  elements/            app-* elements, auto-imported
  pages/
    _layout.ts         root layout, <gemkit-outlet> renders child routes
    _error.ts          error page / 404
    index.ts           /
    blog/
      _layout.ts       nested layout, kept while navigating within /blog/*
      [slug].ts        /blog/:slug
      [slug].server.ts server-only load / actions
      [...rest].ts     /blog/*
  locales/
    en.json            default language
    zh.json            /zh/*

Data loading: isomorphic load + server modules

A page's load is isomorphic: it runs during SSR and client navigation. Server-only code goes in a *.server.ts file with the same name. It's never bundled for the client; importing it from client code fails the build:

// src/pages/blog/[slug].server.ts
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

export async function load({ params }) {
  return { markdown: await readFile(`content/${params.slug}.md`, 'utf8') };
}

// src/pages/blog/[slug].ts
@page<{ slug: string }, { markdown: string }>({
  load: ({ data }) => parseMarkdown(data.markdown),
  title: ({ data }) => data.title,
})
export default class PostPage extends GemElement {
  @property data?: { html: string };

  @template()
  #content = () => html`<article .innerHTML=${this.data?.html}></article>`;
}
  • First load: data is embedded in the HTML as JSON and used during hydration, no extra request
  • Client navigation: Gemkit fetches <page path>/__data.json with the data of the page and all its layouts
  • Prerendering: data files are written next to pages, so client navigation works on static hosting too

Requests, cookies, redirects and forms

In *.server.ts, load can read the request and cookies and redirect in one line, and actions handle form submissions, just like SvelteKit:

// src/pages/article/[slug].server.ts (from the RealWorld app)
export async function load(ctx) {
  const [{ article }, { comments }] = await Promise.all([
    api(ctx, `articles/${ctx.params.slug}`),
    api(ctx, `articles/${ctx.params.slug}/comments`),
  ]);
  // markdown is converted on the server, marked and sanitize-html never reach the client
  return { article: { ...article, body: sanitizeHtml(await marked(article.body)) }, comments };
}

export const actions = {
  deleteArticle: async (ctx) => {
    await api(ctx, `articles/${ctx.params.slug}`, 'DELETE');
    redirect(303, '/');
  },
};

API routes are plain *.server.ts modules exporting GET, POST, etc., with a typed $gemkit/api client.

Server elements: islands with Web Components

This is where Gemkit and Web Components fit together best. A page can mix three kinds of elements:

Decorator Server Client
@server() rendered no code, no hydration; code and dependencies stay out of the client bundle
@lazy({ on }) rendered shows server HTML, loads code and hydrates on interaction / visible / idle
@client() tag only renders normally, the module can use browser-only code 
@customElement('app-like-button')
@lazy({ on: 'interaction' })
class AppLikeButtonElement extends GemElement {}

By default @lazy loads on the first interaction, and the event that triggered loading (click, pointerdown, etc.) is re-dispatched to the original target, so the first click is not lost. Rarely used parts like like-buttons and comment boxes don't cost first-load JS.

@server() can also mark a method or field. It runs during SSR, the resulting state is output with the element and restored during hydration, and the first run on the client is skipped, so data isn't fetched twice:

@customElement('app-comments')
class AppCommentsElement extends GemElement {
  #state = createState({ comments: [] as Comment[] });

  // Server: awaited before output, state is sent with the element
  // Client: restored on first load and skipped; runs when mounted after client navigation
  @server()
  @mounted()
  #load = async () => this.#state({ comments: await fetchComments() });

  @template()
  #content = () => html`${this.#state.comments.map((c) => html`<p>${c.text}</p>`)}`;
}

Rendering modes: SSG, SSR, ISR

  • Every page is prerendered at build time by default (SSG) and can be deployed to any static host
  • Pages that read cookies or the request export prerender = false and are rendered per request by gemkit start
  • export const revalidate = 60 enables ISR: rendered and cached on the first request, then re-rendered in the background when stale

Also: links prefetch modules, data and server element HTML on hover; back/forward restores from a history cache without requests and restores scroll position; src/locales generates locale-prefixed routes.

GemBook now runs on Gemkit, so Gem's documentation sites finally have full SSR/SSG. The Gemkit docs are built with it.

RealWorld comparison

To check whether Gemkit holds up in a real app, I implemented RealWorld (Conduit, a Medium clone) and compared it with the SvelteKit, Nuxt and Next.js implementations on the same local backend, seed data and theme CSS.

Apple M2, 16 GB, Node v25.8.1, Lighthouse median of 5 runs.

Client JS (gzip)

Home Article JS requests (home)
Gemkit 25.9 KB 25.9 KB 2
SvelteKit 44.0 KB 43.3 KB 23
Nuxt 85.8 KB 85.5 KB 15
Next.js 103.5 KB 126.5 KB 8

Lighthouse, home (mobile, simulated throttling)

Score FCP LCP TBT
Gemkit 100 906 ms 1361 ms 0
SvelteKit 100 1285 ms 1671 ms 0
Nuxt 99 1656 ms 1806 ms 0
Next.js 96 908 ms 2022 ms 4

SSR throughput (autocannon, 20 connections, median of 5 rounds)

Home req/s Article req/s
Gemkit 1382 1377
SvelteKit 1437 1388
Nuxt 1042 1169
Next.js 317 359

Other

Client navigation (home → article) Source lines Official e2e passed
Gemkit 53 ms 968 84 / 91
SvelteKit 78 ms 1143 6 / 93
Nuxt 95 ms 711 86 / 91
Next.js 86 ms 2712 60 / 91

How to read this:

  • JS size: Gemkit's home page ships about 59% of SvelteKit's JS, 30% of Nuxt's and 25% of Next's. Web Components are a browser feature, so the framework runtime is small.
  • Lighthouse: Gemkit and SvelteKit both score 100; Gemkit's FCP is about 400 ms faster.
  • SSR throughput: Gemkit and SvelteKit are roughly even (SvelteKit is 1–4% higher), 18–33% above Nuxt and about 4x Next. Both are close to the shared backend's limit; Gemkit spent about 44% of the time waiting for the backend.
  • e2e: the remaining Gemkit failures are mostly environment issues (slow external images, the backend only returning popular tags). The SvelteKit and Next community implementations predate the e2e conventions (different routes), so their low pass rates don't mean missing features.

Building RealWorld was also a good round of dogfooding. It exposed and fixed several issues: load couldn't access the request, query-only navigation didn't re-run load, and children hydrating before their parents caused mismatches. CPU profiling found that every route match created a new URLPattern (now cached, with plain string comparison for patterns without parameters) and an extra TextEncoderStream. After those fixes, home page throughput went from 661 to about 1380 req/s.

Code, reproduction steps and raw data are on GitHub. Corrections are welcome.

Summary

Gem went from client-only to a full SSR framework in three steps:

  1. jsdom prototype: serialization (Declarative Shadow DOM) and hydration without recreating the DOM, proving SSR works for Web Components
  2. gem-ssr: no jsdom, string rendering + request isolation + streaming
  3. Gemkit: on top of gem-ssr and inspired by Next.js / SvelteKit, with file-based routing, layouts, load/actions, server elements, SSG/ISR and i18n

The result is a framework built on web standards, with ~26 KB of first-load JS and performance on par with SvelteKit. If you're interested in Web Components, give it a try:

npm create gemkit@latest my-app
  • GitHub: https://github.com/mantou132/gem
  • Gemkit docs: https://gemkit.gemjs.org/en/
  • Gem docs: https://gemjs.org
